$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}: &={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}: &={R}_{4}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}: &={R}_{3}+\left(-\frac{8}{5}\right){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}: &={R}_{4}+\frac{18}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. Therefore, we get the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{2} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which has only the zero solution $x_1=x_2=0.$

It states that $$ e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta. $$ With Euler's formula, we can write any complex number $z$ in three equivalent ways. Letting $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\textrm{arg}(z),$ we have the following:
**** Cartesian Polar Exponential
$z$ $x+\textrm{i}y$ $r\left( \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta\right)$ $re^{\textrm{i}\theta}$
For instance, if $z=1+\textrm{i},$ then we have $$ \begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}, \\ \theta & =\text{arg}(z)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{1}\right)=\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned} $$ So, the complex number $z=1+\textrm{i}$ can be written in exponential form as $$ z=\sqrt{2}e^{\textrm{i}\pi/4}. $$ When $\theta=\pi,$ we have a special case: $$ e^{\textrm{i}\pi} = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{\textrm{i}\pi} +1=0 $$ The equation $e^{\textrm{i}\pi} +1=0$ is called **Euler's identity**. We say that two vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}=-4\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=-4{a}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{a}_{1}-4{a}_{1} & =0 \\ 4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=0
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=4$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

$$
D_1(y) = x\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} +x^2y
$$

$$

$$

Since derivatives distribute over sums, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1})+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(b{y}_{2})+{x}^{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =ax\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}_{1})+bx\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}_{2})+a{x}^{2}{y}_{1}+b{x}^{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =a\underbrace{\left(x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}{y}_{1}\right)}_{{D}_{1}({y}_{1})}+b\underbrace{\left(x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}{y}_{2}\right)}_{{D}_{1}({y}_{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, since $D_1(ay_1 + by_2) = aD_1(y_1) + bD_1(y_2),$ the operator $D_1$ is linear.
